newsitem.title: LESOTHO: Namibia to eventually use Okavango water, official.
newsitem.headline: Namibia to eventually use Okavango water, official.

text.p: Good rains in Namibia have put on hold emergency plans to pump river water feeding Botswana's environmentally sensitive Okavango Delta, but it will eventually be inevitable, a Namibian official said on Tuesday.

Over 100 southern African and European Union delegates were gathered in the capital of the tiny mountain kingdom of Lesotho for a conference on sharing water, a scarce and precious resource in the arid and semi-arid region.

Plans to draw water out of the Okavango River to supply the Namibian capital of Windhoek and its central area have raised the ire of environmentalists, said Piet Heyns, a director in Namibia's agriculture and water ministry.

But it was the cheapest and most viable option the large sparsely populated country had, he told Reuters, adding that less than one percent of the average 10 billion cubic metres of water flowing into the delta yearly would be pumped out.

"By the year 2000 it will be inevitable that we will have to go to the Okavango because there is no other way to meet the demand for water, and our demands are insignificant if one considers how much water flows into the delta," Heyns said.

Recent good rains in Namibia broke a four-year drought, giving the country enough water for up to three years -- meaning a more in-depth environmental assessment could be made before it became inevitable to pump water, he said.
"There is a misconception that if we pumped water from the Okavango that we would do it all the time and not use our internal resources. We won't pump a drop of water if it's not necessary," he said.
Heyns insisted the issue had not affected the relationship between the Namibian and Botswanan governments.
"There has never been any conflict whatsoever. There is a full and mutual understanding between the two governments as far as water resource management is concerned," he said.
Botswanan minister of mineral resources and water affairs, David Magang told Reuters his government did not oppose studies into utilising water from the delta.
"We are interested in a joint study of the delta because it would give us a better idea of how much we could use if the possibility arose," he said.
Botswana currently relies on underground water and does not use water from the delta. He said ways were being looked at to exploit its tourist potential without damaging the system.
